one_liner: Rust rewrite of Postgres with columnar tables; claims a ClickBench lead over ClickHouse, but ClickBench removed it as benchmark-tuned.
what_it_does: pgrust is a from-scratch Rust reimplementation of the PostgreSQL 18 server (v0.3 reports 18.6) that speaks the Postgres wire protocol and SQL dialect and passes Postgres's 46,066-test regression suite. You run it as a standalone server and connect with psql or libpq; it still borrows C Postgres's initdb and share directory. The analytics numbers apply only to tables created USING pgrcolumnar (called cbstore before v0.3), an append-only columnar table access method loaded through COPY. It is not a ClickHouse replacement: the SQL is Postgres's, and existing Postgres extensions do not load.
how_it_is_fast: Analytics run on a vectorized, push-based executor that processes batches of about 1,024 rows, fuses operators and uses ARM64 NEON SIMD, plus a copy-and-patch JIT (hand-encoded AArch64 stencils instead of LLVM, about 5 us to compile) for expressions and tuple deforming on aarch64 only. pgrcolumnar row groups use dictionary encoding, DeltaFor integers and a per-chunk LZ4/Zstd choice, carry zone-map, NDV/HLL and zero-count footer statistics, and are read by mmap outside the buffer cache; a per-granule condition cache and answers taken straight from part metadata let some queries skip the scan entirely. The author credits an adaptive hash table (L2-resident or out-of-cache layout, chosen by cardinality) as a major ClickBench win. For OLTP the README credits threads instead of processes, work-stealing parallel query, PGO plus fat LTO, and pipelined fsync.
when_to_use: Trying out a Postgres-wire-compatible server for read-mostly analytics over one wide, append-only fact table, loaded once via COPY, on AWS Graviton4 (c8g). This is the only setup the published numbers cover.

Read-heavy OLTP experiments on Graviton4 where the kit's 1.25-1.40x sysbench oltp_read_only throughput over PostgreSQL 18.3 matters. That figure is for a 300 GB dataset on i8g.xlarge with a PGO build, and it only helps if you can run non-production software.
Studying alternative Postgres internals: a copy-and-patch JIT, thread-per-connection backends, a query scheduler and built-in OOM killer, and Kani proofs of function-level parity with C Postgres.
when_not_to_use: Any data you cannot lose. The README says it is not production-ready ('Keep Postgres as the source of truth'). The issue tracker shows recent panics in logical replication, SERIALIZABLE and crash recovery, and the thread-per-backend model weakens Postgres's crash isolation (issue #67).

Ad-hoc analytics. ClickBench's maintainer found that the v0.4-preview columnar engine refuses query shapes outside the 43 ClickBench queries, with no fallback: SELECT MIN(URL) FROM hits and AVG(UserID + 1) both error. The public v0.3 source ships hand-lowered plans for all 43 queries. Use ClickHouse, DuckDB or DataFusion instead.

Columnar tables that need UPDATE, DELETE, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT, row locking, CLUSTER, TID or bitmap scans, backward scans or TABLESAMPLE. pgrcolumnar refuses all of these, and TOASTed or compressed input values have to arrive through COPY.

x86-64, non-Graviton ARM, or Windows. The JIT targets neoverse-v2 only, the published binaries are generic, no x86 ClickBench row was submitted because 'there is no JIT on x86-64', and Windows is unsupported.

Workloads with many small statements, or that need Postgres extensions. Issue #117 measured 1.44-2.04x slower than PostgreSQL 18.6 per statement on x86-64, mostly planner overhead. The kit's pgbench read-write result is near parity (~1.03x). PostGIS-style C extensions, PL/Python, PL/Perl and PL/Tcl do not work.

integration.form: standalone server binary (Postgres wire protocol), not a library: prebuilt Linux/macOS binaries, Docker image malisper/pgrust:v0.3, or cargo build --bin postgres
integration.dependencies: At runtime, PostgreSQL 18 client tools (initdb, psql) and a Postgres share/timezone directory, set through PGRUST_PGSHAREDIR and PGRUST_TZDIR. RE2 (libre2) is required for release builds from source.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.96.0 (pinned in rust-toolchain.toml; LLVM 22 needed for aarch64 thin-LTO)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 and aarch64, macOS arm64 and x86-64, plus a WebAssembly (wasip1) build for the browser demo. The JIT and the tuned performance are aarch64 Graviton4 (neoverse-v2) only. No Windows.
integration.thread_safety: Server process with one OS thread per connection in a single address space, instead of Postgres's process per backend. Caught panics go through crash handling; memory-safety faults kill the whole server by design (issue #67).
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it is closer to a drop-in for PostgreSQL than for ClickHouse. It speaks the Postgres wire protocol and SQL, and the Docker image mirrors the official postgres image's env vars and volumes. ClickHouse SQL, table engines and clients do not apply. Postgres extensions do not load. Columnar tables must be declared USING pgrcolumnar and are append-only.

gotchas: On 2026-09-22 ClickBench's maintainer removed every pgrust row (ClickBench PR #2165). The v0.4-preview binary contained per-query kernels (irprobe q00.rs...q36.rs) and plan matchers named after ClickBench queries, and hot runs replayed cached filter verdicts. Q20 took 10.8 s cold, then 11 ms on the second run; the same query with a new constant took 283 ms. The v0.3 source's clickbench.ron answers Q0-Q3, Q6, Q19 and Q29 from metadata, and Q20's hot rep is 'pure fold over cached verdicts'.

The headline figures disagree with each other. The README says 18.5% ahead of ClickHouse. The kit says ~0.93 combined (~7% ahead, stock settings). Its scorer mentions '8.6% ahead'. The v0.2 ClickBench submission said mid-teens with pgrust.condition_cache on and ~4% with it off. All of these use pgrust's own 'combined' weighting, not ClickBench's metric.

The README's benchmarks/ link 404s on main; the harness only exists on archive/v0.2-main-2026-09-15. It assumes a GNU/Linux userland and a gp2 EBS volume (gp3 costs ~12 combined points). The kit never runs ClickBench on C PostgreSQL, so 'hundreds of times faster than PostgreSQL' is not measured by the harness.
Starting the server needs ulimit -s 65520, RUST_MIN_STACK=32 MiB, io_method=sync and max_stack_depth=60000. pgrust has no initdb of its own yet. SQL written for v0.2 with USING cbstore fails on v0.3.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Hydra Columnar puts a columnar AM inside real PostgreSQL, and ClickHouse, Databend or DataFusion are general engines, so pick one of those for real analytics. pgrust only makes sense for evaluating one experimental Postgres-compatible server that pairs faster read-only OLTP with a columnar AM on Graviton4. Unlike Umbra's or Firebolt Core's, pgrust's ClickBench rows were withdrawn.
verified_claims_summary: The published kit (archive/v0.2 branch) runs the 43 ClickBench queries on pgrcolumnar on a c8g.4xlarge (Graviton4, 500 GiB gp2), built with rustc 1.96, fat LTO, PGO and -Ctarget-cpu=neoverse-v2. It scores the run against a vendored 2026-07-19 ClickHouse leaderboard row using pgrust's own hot^0.6*cold^0.2*load^0.1*size^0.1 weighting and lands at ~0.93: much faster cold, slightly faster hot, slower load, larger on disk. The only real head-to-head is OLTP against PostgreSQL 18.3 on i8g.xlarge: sysbench oltp_read_only at 300 GB gives 1.25-1.40x (20-30 points less without PGO), and pgbench read-write gives ~1.03x.
status_note: Actively developed: pushes through 2026-09-18, v0.3 released, and a v0.4-preview binary whose source is unpublished. It is AGPL-3.0, not accepting pull requests and self-described as not production-ready, so treat it as a Docker-image experiment, not a component to vendor.
